headline: Minogue's record $19.5 million doesn't dent Healey's Massachusetts margin
dek: A Republican executive paid for most of his own campaign and set the state's spending records. A Democratic governors' super PAC and a friend's super PAC also spent money. Gov. Maura Healey still won by 27 points.
summary: Massachusetts: Mike Minogue spent a record $19.5 million of his own money and lost to Maura Healey by 27 points.

paras.text: Michael Minogue, a Republican from Hamilton, set every campaign-spending record Massachusetts keeps. He put $19.5 million of his own money into his campaign, the most any statewide candidate in Massachusetts has given himself. His campaign reported spending more than $21.4 million, also a record and well above the roughly $13.9 million that former lieutenant governor Kerry Healey spent in 2006. On Nov. 3, Gov. Maura Healey beat him 1,625,487 votes to 911,234, a margin of 27.2 points, according to Associated Press results published by The New York Times. That works out to about $21.40 of Minogue's own money for each vote he got.

The U.S. Senate race drew almost no money. The Federal Election Commission data available to The Watch shows no outside spending reported for Sen. Edward Markey or his Republican opponent, John Deaton, and the FEC's figures for the candidates themselves have not been read yet. Markey won by 31.2 points.

Most of the Republican money came from Minogue himself. In September, Boston.com reported that he had put in $15.8 million of his own since October 2025, while outside donors had given only about $1.28 million that year. State law caps what one person can give a candidate's campaign at $1,000 a year. A super PAC, by contrast, can take individual contributions of any size.
Healey raised her money under that cap. The Boston Globe reported that she had spent nearly $6.4 million since announcing her reelection run in February 2025.

Two super PACs registered with the state also spent money in the race. The one backing Minogue, Massachusetts First, is led by Rob Neuner, chief executive of Boost Oxygen, a company based in Connecticut. State House News Service described Neuner as Minogue's childhood friend and as the PAC's chairman and largest donor. Other donors included Matthew Daniels, a real estate executive at JLL, and his wife, Jennifer, who together gave $100,000. The PAC had spent $1.3 million since late June.

The Democratic side had the Commonwealth for Tomorrow Independent Expenditure PAC. The Democratic Governors Association gave this super PAC $1.085 million. According to WBUR, the PAC had spent $585,000 against Minogue since late June.

Healey's message was that Minogue would bring President Donald Trump's agenda to Massachusetts. Her early attack ads called him "MAGA Mike." The Boston Herald reported that the ad cost hundreds of thousands of dollars, paid for by her campaign and the Democratic State Committee. Her six-figure spot "Not for Sale" ran statewide on broadcast and cable TV and on digital and streaming platforms. In it, Healey says Minogue gave more than a million dollars to Trump and supports ICE (the federal immigration agency), Trump's health care cuts and limits on abortion rights. The Democratic governors' super PAC spent most of its money online. It paid for polling, research and a $250,000 digital ad buy in mid-October for videos calling Minogue a "MAGA mega-donor."

Minogue's own ads argued that Healey's administration rewarded insiders. The Globe reported that he spent nearly $5 million on ads in September. His statewide TV ad "Power Corrupts" told viewers that "Healey's insiders do better. You get the bill." In September, Massachusetts First ran its own statewide ad, a montage of Healey mentioning Trump followed by the charge that she won't take responsibility for the state's problems.

In the final weeks, Massachusetts First stopped aiming at Healey and started aiming at Andrea James, an independent candidate running to her left. The Globe counted $542,812 the PAC spent on mailers, texts and digital ads calling James a "do-everything socialist" and the "Massachusetts Mamdani." One mailer went to households with registered Democrats. It showed James promising "Housing for all. Healthcare for all. Childcare for all." Neuner said James shows "the direction Massachusetts is going, and people should be aware of that." A political analyst, Cluverius, told GBH News the ads "seem designed to elevate James as a spoiler to shave votes from Healey."

The Senate race had a smaller super PAC effort for Deaton. The Globe reported that a Boston voter had just received a text from a pro-Deaton super PAC. The writer Molly White's newsletter, Citation Needed, counted about $700,000 for Deaton from Commonwealth Unity Fund, a super PAC funded by the cryptocurrency industry that exists only to support him. That spending does not yet appear in the FEC data The Watch has read.

No. Using the totals reported by late October, Minogue's campaign and his super PAC together outspent Healey's campaign and hers by more than three to one. He still lost by 27.2 points. Healey's margin was 1.9 points wider than the Democrats' margin in the state in the 2024 presidential race. His share of the vote, about 34 percent, was close to the nearly 35 percent the 2022 Republican nominee, Geoff Diehl, won with far less money.
The Senate race had almost no reported spending and moved further toward the Democrats. Markey ran 5.9 points ahead of the 2024 presidential margin, three times the governor's race shift.

A Boston Globe opinion columnist argued that Minogue couldn't get past two things: his support for Trump in a state where Trump has a 25 percent approval rating, and his personal opposition to abortion rights. Minogue's view of all that spending was that it left him independent. On the last weekend he told supporters, "Which means when I get elected, nobody owns me."
